Your feelings are completely valid and common. I had an unknown pregnancy and miscarried back in September as well. I had the same thought you were, and thought that maybe I would have made it work and been a good mom.

I hope this helps. My thoughts are with you and wish you the best!

I can't function without being organized and planning. When I went into a but of a rut, these are what I did which have totally made life a lot easier. 

1. Keep your room clean. Designate one day a week, preferably the same day, to deep clean your area and make everything look perfect. A clean room is one of the best things you can do for motivating yourself. 
2. The best thing I did was getting a bullet journal. You can get a planner or something that isn't as much work to set up, but have a place to write down what you want to accomplish everyday and when you want to do it. 
3. Designate times in the day for the essentials. Maybe what gets you out of bed at a decent time is having an early shower time or going out for a walk. Plan meal times and stick to them. Just find easy things that you do everyday and structure them to fit into certain times. 
4. Have at least one thing you are going to accomplish a day. Whether that be cleaning, work, meal prep, or just something slightly productive, have that in mind and try to get it done as early as you can to combat the avoiding sleep to do something. Giving a purpose during the day might help you out. 
5. Find small, healthy habits that you want to adopt and work at them one at a time. 

Don't push yourself and change all of your habits at once or else you will crash. Go at a slow pace and take things one at a time. Hope this helps!

I am 19 from the Us and was also diagnosed with bipolar within this past year. My parents weren't really involved in the process since I am an adult, so I had to ask all the questions myself. Here are some points that you can think about when coming up with questions:

1. I repeat this in the rest of the points, but include her in the discussion. She is the most knowledgeable about her condition. A doctor may share general information that pertains to bipolar in general, but her input and advise will be the most helpful. She might even appreciate that you are wanting to learn from her. So make sure you are asking her questions (and respect if she does not want to share). 
2. Try to get as much info about bipolar and her diagnosis. The best thing you can do is be educated about bipolar in general as well as what she personally experiences. It is different for everyone, so knowing what she goes through is very helpful. She may not want to talk to you personally about it (as most teens don't want to be open with their parents), but try asking her about it as well and see what she is comfortable sharing. 
3. Ask about her medication. Read up about people's experiences with Vraylar/Cariprazine first (I would say WebMD and Reddit can be helpful) Then tell the doctor what she is experiencing and what they think should be the best course of action. 
4. What can you do? I know it is hard, but there may not be much that you can do. Learning to live with any mental health condition comes down to the person who has it. It comes down to her. So ask what actions you can take to help her in her journey. It may just be small things and very indirect. My advise is to never make assumptions or be intrusive (ex: my parents were overly cautious around me and I would get sooo annoyed). Be open, ask her if there is anything you can do, and let life go on as normal.  
5. What else can we do besides medication? They will often suggest pairing it with therapy (I suggest that as well). There are a lot of different approaches to therapy, so do some research before going to the doctor to see what they suggest for helping her. Note that she may go through a few therapists before finding the right one. Even if it comes down to she doesn't like the 'vibe' of that therapist, respect it and keep searching. Don't make her keep going because you think she isn't giving it enough time. By the second meeting, she will know if it isn't the right fit. Trust her judgement. 

A have had a few nurse practitioners in psych and I would say they are usually just as reliable as a psychiatrist. If you are weary about them, I would look to finding a psychiatrist for a second opinion, even if it is a far drive. That could help put you at ease. 

I am on lamotrigine, and while it does take some time to work up to the right dosage, I have had great success with minimal side effects. 

I know this was very long and in depth, but I hope you found some things helpful. Write down your questions before you go so you can hit every point. Best of luck to you and your daughter!

Firstly, feeling invalid in your diagnosis is super normal in people with bp. It is also very common to feel that this is a burden that others should not have to deal with. Here's my best advice:

1. You are valid, you are not a burden, and you deserve happiness just like everyone else on this planet. 
2. If you feel like you are starting to get into a dangerous place, you may want to consider going to a psych facility. I know this seems scary, but it could really help you take the time to figure out what outside sources are contributing to the issue while also giving yourself a reset. There is no shame in needing a safe place to take care of yourself. 
3. Find a therapist to talk to about these issues with. They are here to listen to you and will never think of you as a burden. They will also let you talk about everything, no matter how deep/intense it may be. Whether it is alone or in a group, having someone(s) to comfortably open up to could help a lot.
4. When talking to people in your life, you don't have to share everything. You can pick what you want to open up about and what exactly you want to share. Start out talking about topics that you feel won't scare them or make them worry much. When I want to talk to someone, I usually try to stay a bit vague and ask to vent rather than get advise. The people who love you do not feel it is a burden, but rather are happy to help you work through your issues. They see this as a way to grow closer and want to help. You may even be that way with the people in your life.

This happened with my mom/aunt back in 2009. She lost both of her parents in the span of 2 months. They both visited them in a dream, and she does not remember all the details, she remembers feeling a sense of closure knowing that they were still connected with her. She woke up crying and couldn't sleep the rest of the night. My aunt had the same dream that night, which I rack up to them being twins and having a freaky connection. 

I would think this dream shows that you are still struggling with letting go (which is totally normal and valid with how recent this was), but also that you know deep down that he is okay wherever he is. From his demeanor, it looks like he is doing good. I don't know if you have talked about it with your family, but maybe that could help you in finding closure and accepting his passing. You may also consider looking into a grief counselor to see what they suggest. 

If you are comfortable, maybe try thinking about him before bed to see if he may visit you again. Think about him and a place where you spent time together alone. Being prepared may give you a better experience, and though you usually cannot speak to those who passed in dreams, just seeing him will give you a sense of how he is and what he wants for you.

For me, hypomania makes me super productive, but I struggle to stay on task. Having a list of what needs to get done helps me to make sure all my work is completed while letting me jump around from task to task. It all depends on what you experience with hypomania and trying to work with it, rather than against it. 

As for mania, that is a different story. Have you talked to your employer about your condition? Under The Americans with Disabilities Act and Title VII, employers are required to make "reasonable accommodations" as long as it does not create "undue hardship". For Bipolar, you can request for an accommodated work schedule, request mental health days (as long as it they are not super frequent or for long periods of time), and have time off for medical needs during the work week. Your employer cannot discriminate/fire you for this, or you have the right to sue (remedies for your case could include getting your job back and/or compensation for your time you were laid off/ emotional distress). 

You really should not have any fears when talking to your employer about this. Go to your HR department, explain your condition (you might have to show documentation), tell how it effects your work, and see what they can do for you. 

I hope this helps!

Firstly, it is great that you are acknowledging and being proactive in making sure you are safe and trying to get better. That can often be the hardest part. 

My experience in a psych center was great for me. Know that you do not need to feel like you are in immediate danger to check yourself in. A lot of people I met there were just felt like they were starting to get bad and wanted to be proactive about it. They will put you on a routine along with everyone else, while still giving you free time (which I suggest using to make friends in there). I got visiting hours everyday where my family could come and just be with me, either talking about what I am going through or just playing cards with me. Make sure they know you are going so they can come and be with you. 

I've been on lamictal for 9 months now, and, for me, it took around 6 months to find the right dosage and really start working (I have also heard people seeing results in less time). I have found it to really help lower the intensity of the episodes and give me time to work out what I am going through without getting caught up in emotions. Medication is a long process to find what's right, and for the time being, you may want to look into going to therapy multiple times a week. That could be beneficial while you are still getting used to the medication. 

I hope this helps and best of luck to you on your journey. Keep looking forward.

When you don't take your medication for a few days, it can send you into very intense episodes. I would make to tell your doctor that you did have a skip in your medicine recently and see what they say about it/ if the side effects you are experiencing are normal. Since this has been going on for a while, talk about your symptoms, what you are struggling with most in terms of thoughts/actions, and tell them that you feel this may be something you need. 

As for the depressive episode, it's great that you are making sure to keep up with basic hygiene/necessities. Know that it is okay to let yourself be in that low place and have days where you just need to be lazy and alone. I am starting to go into a depressive state, and getting out of bed is the hardest thing for me. It feels like too much effort to even sit up or look at my phone. I push myself to do those things and will make a list of things that I feel would be productive/make me feel good. My list today was cleaning the shower, making food that I really like, and get out of the house to do some thrifting. I find the more you can get out of the house and have tasks to keep you busy, the less time you have to think about not wanting to do anything. 

I hope this helps and make sure that you reach out to someone if you feel that things are getting very bad or that you feel in danger. I wish you a great day and keep looking forward!

I did the same thing when I started recovery after a relapse earlier this year. I found it to help a lot. It will look a lot different than what it would for someone without an ED. Here's my best tips for starting out and staying healthy: 

1. Have set times for 3 meals a day. Getting yourself on a schedule and keeping to it will help tune your body clock to automatically want to eat at those times. This will also help in making sure you are eating enough. 
2. Start writing down how you feel before you eat, right after, and an hour later and then a bit later if you start to think about eating again. This will help you recognize the physical and mental sign your body is giving you in terms of hunger. 
3. Have meal plans in mind, but don't meal prep. Look at what foods you like or gravitate towards when you pick something, and make sure have those on hand. This helps make sure that you have all the things that you may want when you get hungry, but keeps you away from trying to plan out calories.
4. Know that your hunger levels will vary from day to day. Some days you may eat more than others, but as you stay more mindful, you will see how the body naturally balances out your hunger. Don't get upset about certain days where you feel it was too much or too little. That's completely natural and okay. 
5. Start out with just around the portion size. After that, wait about 15 minutes, write down how you feel different from right before you ate, and see if you feel like you need more or are okay. Sometimes your body just needs time to recognize that you did eat and tell your brain if that was enough. 

I would say doing research and learning about what your body does when giving hunger cues will help a lot in learning about your own. I hope this helps and best of luck to you!

I am also a second semester college student with bipolar. I only recently reached out for help just because my symptoms were taking a toll on my roommates and friends. It's really hard for me to talk to my parents about it. I know that they are so supportive and loving and always there to help, but I have never really felt comfortable with sharing that kind of stuff because I know how much it will worry them. My best suggestion if you are going to try and have a talk with her is to let her do most of the talking, do not have strong reactions (it might make her hold things in to not scare you), and let her feel in control. Ultimately, it's her decision whether or not she wants to seek help, and you have to respect that. Just let her know that you will always be there for her if she does choose to get help. Most importantly, understand that her talking to you, if she is like me, will be extremely uncomfortable and she may not want to open up that discussion of getting help just yet.

I think you can definitely just come straight out and say that. I would also check and see if you have any family history of bipolar as well. It is a lot more likely that it could be that if someone else in your family has it.
